The Diwali mela was packed and deafening. "Harish, hold my hand!" Devika shouted.
But Harish saw a smiling man with shiny balloons and a bag of sweets. "He's nice!" Harish said, and let go.
Devika, his mother, caught his hand in two steps and pulled him close. "We don't go to people we don't know, even smiley ones."
Near the gate sat a plain-looking woman in a grey uniform at the lost-children desk. Harish hid behind Devika's legs. "She looks scary."
Devika knelt. "She's a helper. If you're ever lost, she's the one to go to."

qa.q: Where did the woman in the grey uniform sit?
qa.a: Near the gate, at the lost-children desk.

qa.q: Why did Harish let go of Devika's hand for the man with balloons?
qa.a: The shiny balloons and sweets gave him a happy, excited feeling, so the man felt nice and safe to him.

qa.q: What could Devika do before the next crowded fair?
qa.a: She could show Harish the helper desk first and practise together: if lost, go to someone in uniform at the desk, never to anyone offering treats.

qa.q: What was it like for Devika when Harish let go?
qa.a: She was frightened for a moment, which is why she caught him in two steps and held him close.

grounding: Shows a young child trusting a friendly-seeming stranger because it feels good and fearing a plain-looking helper, with his mother stepping in.

passage:
Monday, in the chilly first week of January. Darshan finished his art homework in ten minutes, humming. "Drawing is easy, and it's useful. Artists are everywhere." Then he opened his maths book and groaned. "Fractions are impossible. Nobody even uses them."
Wednesday. His cousin Saurabh asked, "How do you know fractions are useless?" Darshan shrugged. "I just hate them. So they are."
Saturday. Saurabh sat beside him while he drew a kite. "To make both sides match, you split it in half. Then quarters for the tail pattern." Darshan stopped, pencil in the air. "That's... fractions?" He frowned at the kite, then at the maths book. "Maybe they're not totally pointless."

qa.q: What did Darshan draw on Saturday?
qa.a: A kite.

qa.q: Why does Darshan think fractions are useless?
qa.a: He dislikes them and feels frustrated, so the feeling hands him a quick answer: hard and pointless.

qa.q: What helped Darshan see fractions differently?
qa.a: Saurabh linked fractions to something Darshan loves, splitting the kite into halves and quarters.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Darshan's "I just hate them. So they are"?
qa.a: Saurabh seems amused but wants to show him that hating something doesn't decide whether it is useful.

grounding: Shows a child who finds a subject he likes easy and useful and one he dislikes hard and pointless.

passage:
Dussehra fair, Saturday night
Best night ever and also embarrassing. The giant swing was AMAZING. The operator didn't check if the safety bar clicked, and ours was loose, but I didn't care. It felt so fun that it felt safe, if that makes sense.
Mahima didn't think so. She pulled me off after one round and went straight to the man at the fair office. He stopped the ride and fixed the bar in front of everyone. I was so annoyed.
On the way out she asked about the climbing wall at school next week. I said no way, too dangerous. She laughed. "You'll have a harness and a teacher holding the rope. The swing had a broken bar."
She's right, and I hate it. The fun thing felt safe, the scary thing felt deadly, and the facts were the other way round.
Anand

qa.q: What did the man at the fair office do?
qa.a: He stopped the ride and fixed the bar in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did the giant swing feel safe to Anand?
qa.a: It was so thrilling that the good feeling made it seem safe, even with a loose safety bar.

qa.q: What question could Anand ask before judging a risk next time?
qa.a: What are the facts, like a loose bar versus a harness and a teacher on the rope, rather than how fun or scary it feels?

qa.q: How did Mahima see the swing and the climbing wall?
qa.a: Mahima judged them by the facts: the swing with the broken bar was the real danger, and the wall with a harness was the safer one.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging risk by how thrilling or scary something feels rather than by the facts.

passage:
Christmas Eve, hostel room
Two offers. The Chennai logistics firm pays better, has proper training, and Karthik's cousin says the team is kind. The Bengaluru startup has a tiny office and a founder who laughed at my joke in the interview.
I knew in about four seconds that I wanted Bengaluru. It just felt right.
Then I spent the whole evening writing reasons: faster learning, more ownership, better city for my future. Karthik read the list and said, "You wrote these after you'd decided, didn't you? You don't even know if they give more ownership."
I got defensive. But he's not wrong. I haven't asked one question about the startup's training or how long it has been running. The reasons arrived after the feeling, like a lawyer hired to defend it.
Tomorrow I'm calling both with the same five questions. Then we'll see if Bengaluru still feels right.
Kamal

qa.q: What did the Bengaluru founder do in the interview?
qa.a: The founder laughed at Kamal's joke.

qa.q: Why did Kamal get defensive when Karthik read the list?
qa.a: Kamal felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, because the reasons had been written after the feeling, to defend it.

qa.q: What is Kamal's plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Calling both companies with the same five questions, so the choice rests on real answers rather than a four-second feeling.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Kamal's list of reasons?
qa.a: Karthik sees them as reasons built after the decision, since Kamal doesn't even know whether the startup gives more ownership.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a job because it just feels right and building the reasons afterwards.

passage:
Last month I nearly signed for a flat in Jayanagar. The rent was fair, the balcony lovely, the landlord charming. But my stomach tightened every time he said, "Don't worry about the paperwork, we'll sort it later."
Once I'd have ignored that feeling or run from it. This time I wrote it down: "Uneasy about landlord. Why?" Then I looked for what supported it and what didn't.
I asked for the agreement a day early and read it with my friend Lakshmi, who had rented nearby. The deposit clause was vague. The previous tenant told me getting her deposit back took eight months.
Against my worry: the building was well kept, and the neighbours liked him.
I asked for the clause to be rewritten. He refused. I walked away, calm rather than scared. I'm Sarika, and my stomach was information, not a verdict.

qa.q: How long did the previous tenant say getting her deposit back took?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel when the landlord said "we'll sort it later", and what was done with that feeling?
qa.a: Sarika felt uneasy, a tightening in the stomach, and wrote it down as a question to check rather than obeying or ignoring it.

qa.q: Which step could anyone copy before a big decision?
qa.a: Writing the feeling down, then looking for evidence on both sides, like reading the agreement with Lakshmi and asking the previous tenant.

qa.q: What was it like for Lakshmi to help read the agreement?
qa.a: Having rented nearby, Lakshmi could offer real experience, and probably felt useful and trusted.

grounding: Shows an adult treating an uneasy feeling as information and checking evidence for and against it before a big decision.

passage:
At the preschool Christmas party, Sudha Ma'am set a plate of star cookies on the low table. Before she could say "one each", Arnab grabbed three.
When Mehul reached for the last star, Arnab shoved him and snatched it. Mehul wailed.
Sudha Ma'am knelt between them. "Arnab, hands are for holding, not pushing." Arnab stared at the cookies in his fists as if he hadn't noticed taking them.
"Let's try a trick," she said. "Before your hands move, freeze like a snowman. Then think." She called, "Snowman!" and Arnab froze, giggling. Slowly, he put two stars back.

qa.q: How many cookies did Arnab grab first?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Arnab stare at the cookies in his fists?
qa.a: He acted on impulse so fast that he seemed surprised, even a little confused, to find the cookies in his hands.

qa.q: Why is Sudha Ma'am's snowman trick useful for Arnab?
qa.a: It gives him a fun, quick pause before his hands move, so his slower thinking can catch up.

qa.q: What was it like for Mehul when Arnab snatched the last star?
qa.a: Mehul was hurt and upset, wailing after being shoved and losing the cookie.

grounding: Shows a preschooler grabbing and pushing on first impulse, and a teacher helping him practise a short pause.

passage:
On Children's Day the school hall was hung with paper flags for the fun quiz. Kishore Sir read out: "A notebook and a pencil cost eleven rupees together. The notebook costs ten rupees more than the pencil. How much is the pencil?"
"One rupee!" shouted half the hall. Nazia's hand shot up too, then stopped halfway.
Last week she had lost a point by blurting. She pressed her lips together and worked it in her head. If the pencil is one, the notebook is eleven, and together that's twelve. Not eleven.
She scribbled on her palm. "Fifty paise," she said.
Kishore Sir smiled. "Why did you stop?"
"The first answer came too fast," Nazia said. "Fast ones feel right, but they trick me."

qa.q: What answer did half the hall shout?
qa.a: "One rupee!"

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when her hand stopped halfway?
qa.a: She felt a flicker of doubt, remembering the point lost last week by blurting, so she was cautious instead of eager.

qa.q: What could Nazia's classmates try with the next trick question?
qa.a: Pause and check the first answer, the way Nazia added the pencil and notebook to see whether they made eleven.

qa.q: How might the children who shouted "One rupee!" feel when Nazia answers?
qa.a: They might feel surprised and a little foolish, since the quick answer felt so obviously right.

grounding: Shows a child catching a wrong first answer to a trick question with a brief pause.

passage:
At the Holi mela in the village, the quiz stage was surrounded by Chaitanya's friends, faces still pink with colour, chanting his name. The quizmaster asked, "A bus leaves at 9:40 and the journey takes 2 hours 50 minutes. When does it arrive?"
Chaitanya slapped the buzzer before the question ended. "Twelve twenty!"
"Wrong," said the quizmaster. The friends groaned.
That night on the quiet roof, his sister Anjali read him the same question from her notebook. Chaitanya closed his eyes, added slowly, and said, "Twelve thirty."
"So why did you say twelve twenty on stage?"
He picked at the colour on his nails. "Everyone was yelling. I just wanted to be first."

qa.q: When did the bus leave in the quiz question?
Why did Chaitanya slap the buzzer before the question ended?
qa.a: With friends chanting his name he felt excited and eager to be first, so he answered on gut instead of working it out.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try the next time he is on stage?
qa.a: Take one breath and add slowly before buzzing, even with friends yelling, since being right matters more than being first.

qa.q: What did Anjali show by asking the question again on the roof?
qa.a: Anjali showed that her brother could solve it calmly, and helped him see that the noise and the friends had pushed him to answer too fast.

grounding: Shows a teenager making a snap choice with friends watching and reasoning carefully when calm.

passage:
In her mother's tailoring shop in the small town, Bhavna matched thread colours without thinking. A customer held up a peacock-blue blouse piece, and Bhavna's hand went straight to the right spool. "That one," she said, and she was right, as usual.
But when a letter came offering her a seat in a two-year design course in Pune, far from home, she didn't trust the rush of "yes!" in her chest.
That night she wrote a list: fees, hostel, who would help Amma in the shop, what the course's past students were doing now. She slept on it. The next day she called her old teacher, and asked Ritu, who had studied in Pune, about the hostel and the classes.
Ritu laughed. "You pick thread in one second, but this takes a week?"
"Thread I can change tomorrow," Bhavna said. "This I can't."

qa.q: Where is the design course Bhavna was offered?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: Why didn't Bhavna trust the rush of "yes!" in her chest?
qa.a: She felt excited, but she was cautious because the move was big, new and hard to undo, unlike choosing thread.

qa.q: What steps did Bhavna use for the big decision?
qa.a: She wrote a list, slept on it, then asked her old teacher and Ritu for advice.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Bhavna's two ways of deciding?
qa.a: Ritu finds it funny at first that thread takes one second and the course takes a week, until Bhavna points out the difference in stakes.

grounding: Shows a young adult trusting quick intuition for familiar small choices and slowing down with a list, sleep and advice for a big new one.

passage:
In our design team I've watched the same thing play out for months. Chetan spends forty minutes choosing between two nearly identical blues for an internal slide, with a comparison table. Anirban, on the other hand, signed a year-long contract with a new printer after one phone call because "the guy sounded solid". The printer missed our first deadline.
Last week I finally said something, gently, over lunch. "Chetan, eight people will see that slide. Pick in two minutes." He laughed, then looked relieved. "Anirban, for the next contract, let's make a checklist together and sleep on it." Anirban bristled, then nodded.
Our lead overheard and made it a team rule: small, reversible choices get a timer; big, new ones get a checklist and a second person.
I'm Sneha, and I don't get it right every time either. But naming the stakes out loud helps.

qa.q: How long does Chetan spend choosing between two blues?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Sneha have felt before speaking up at lunch?
qa.a: Sneha had watched this for months and was probably frustrated but careful, choosing to speak gently rather than criticise.

qa.q: What rule did the lead make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Small, reversible choices get a timer and big, new ones get a checklist and a second person, so effort matches the stakes.

qa.q: How did Chetan and Anirban react to Sneha's suggestions?
qa.a: Chetan laughed and looked relieved, while Anirban bristled at first and then agreed to the checklist.

grounding: Shows a team member noticing one colleague over-analysing a trivial choice and another gut-deciding a big one, and helping both match effort to the stakes.
